blocks.prompt: The Jellyfish With No Brain and No Bones
blocks.text: A jellyfish is not a fish. A fish has bones. A fish has a brain. A jellyfish has neither one. It is almost all water. If you left a jellyfish on the warm sand, it would dry up into a thin little smudge. To swim, a jellyfish squeezes its round bell and pushes water out behind it. Then it opens up again and glides. Its long tentacles hang down like ribbons. Every tentacle is covered in tiny stingers. When a small fish bumps into one, the stingers fire. So a jellyfish never has to chase its dinner. It just waits.

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Is Mostly Water
blocks.text: A jellyfish is about as close to nothing as a living animal can get. It has no brain. It has no heart, no bones, no blood, and no lungs. About 95 parts out of every 100 are plain seawater. What is left is a thin skin wrapped around a layer of clear jelly. So how does it work at all? Instead of a brain, a jellyfish has a nerve net. That is a web of nerves spread through its whole body, a bit like a hair net. No part of it is in charge. The net just passes signals around, and the animal reacts. Instead of chasing its food, a jellyfish waits. Its tentacles are loaded with thousands of stinging cells. Each cell holds a tiny dart, coiled up tight and squeezed under huge pressure. Touch it, and the dart fires in less than a millionth of a second. It is one of the fastest movements in all of nature, and it happens with no thinking at all. Jellyfish were doing this long before there were dinosaurs, and long before there were trees. They have been drifting through the ocean for more than 500 million years.

blocks.prompt: The Cheapest Ride in the Ocean
blocks.text: Build an animal with no bones, no heart, no lungs, and no brain, and you would expect it to be helpless. The jellyfish is the opposite. It is one of the most successful animals in the sea, and part of the reason is that almost nothing it does costs very much. Start with its body. A jellyfish is built from two thin layers of skin with a springy jelly called mesoglea packed between them. It needs no lungs, because oxygen soaks straight through skin that thin. It needs no blood, because nothing inside it is far from the water. It needs no skeleton, because the ocean holds it up for free. Now watch it swim. The bell squeezes shut and shoves a ring of water out behind, which pushes the jellyfish forward. That much is ordinary. The clever part comes next. As the bell relaxes and refills, it makes a second swirl of water underneath itself, and that swirl gives the animal another gentle shove. The jellyfish gets a push on the stroke and a second push on the rest. Scientists who measured this found that a moon jellyfish travels farther on less energy than any other animal they have ever tested. Its life story is odd, too. A jellyfish does not hatch as a jellyfish. It begins as a speck that settles on a rock and grows into a polyp, a small stalk that looks more like a plant. Later the polyp stacks up like a pile of saucers, and the saucers peel off one at a time and swim away. Each saucer becomes a jellyfish. The drifting bell you see at the beach is only the last chapter of a much stranger book.

blocks.prompt: No Brain Required
blocks.text: We tend to assume that intelligence is the reason animals survive. The jellyfish is a standing argument against that assumption. It has no brain and no central nervous system, only a nerve net threaded through its body with no headquarters anywhere in it. It has drifted the ocean for at least 500 million years, which means it was already ancient when the first dinosaur hatched, and it is still here. Consider the weapon it hunts with. Every tentacle carries thousands of stinging cells, and inside each one is a coiled thread packed under pressure many times greater than the air in a car tire. Brush against one and it does not decide to fire. It simply fires, launching its dart in less than a millionth of a second, with an acceleration greater than a bullet leaving a rifle. There is no brain in the loop, because a brain would be too slow. The cell is both the trigger and the gun. Consider the eyes. The box jellyfish carries 24 of them, arranged in clusters around its bell. Some are simple light detectors, but others have a lens, a retina, and a cornea, the same parts your own eye has. It uses them to steer around obstacles and toward light. Nobody knows how it makes sense of 24 views at once with no brain to assemble them. Consider what it does with time. A small jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii, no bigger than your fingernail, can respond to injury or starvation by collapsing back into the polyp stage it came from and starting over. It runs its life cycle backward. It can still be eaten or infected, so it is not truly immortal, but nothing else we know of can simply refuse to finish growing up. Consider the trouble it causes. In 2013, a swarm of moon jellyfish clogged the seawater intake pipes at a nuclear plant in Sweden and forced the operators to shut a reactor down. A creature with no brain switched off a machine built by thousands of engineers. It did not plan it. It just drifted where the current went, in the numbers it has always come in, and the machine was in the way.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Phylum Cnidaria, alive for 500+ million years
Stinging cells are nematocysts inside cnidocytes
Discharge takes under 700 billionths of a second
Box jellies steer using 24 eyes and no brain
Lowest cost of transport ever measured in an animal
Turritopsis dohrnii reverses its life cycle

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Never Needed a Brain
blocks.text: Begin with the list of what a jellyfish does not have. No brain. No heart. No bones, no blood, no lungs, no liver, no spine, no face. Roughly 95 percent of its body is seawater, and the remainder is two thin sheets of cells with a springy jelly called mesoglea packed between them. By almost any standard we use to rank animals, it should be a failure. Instead it is one of the oldest and most durable designs on the planet, drifting the ocean for at least 500 million years, through five mass extinctions that erased far more impressive creatures. It was here before trees. It will very likely be here after us. The absence of a brain is the part that unsettles people, so start there. A jellyfish runs on a nerve net, a mesh of neurons distributed through the whole body with no headquarters and no chain of command. Nothing in it is in charge. Signals simply spread outward and the body responds. This sounds like a limitation until you look at what the animal actually needs to do. It needs to pulse, to sting, to stay upright, and to eat. None of those decisions benefit from committee. Evolution has no obligation to improve on something that already works. Then look at the weapon, which may be the finest piece of machinery any animal owns. Each tentacle carries thousands of cells called cnidocytes, and inside each one sits a capsule called a nematocyst: a coiled, barbed thread held under pressure roughly a hundred and fifty times that of the atmosphere. When a trigger hair is brushed, the capsule does not consult anything. It bursts, and the thread turns inside out and drives into the target in under 700 billionths of a second, at an acceleration of several million times gravity. It is among the fastest movements known in biology. A nervous system could not possibly keep up, which is precisely the point. The jellyfish did not solve the problem of reaction time by thinking faster. It solved it by removing thinking from the loop. Its swimming is just as elegant. The bell contracts and expels a ring of water, which drives the animal forward in the obvious way. But as the bell relaxes, it generates a second vortex beneath itself that delivers a further push at no muscular cost. The jellyfish is therefore propelled during the phase when it is doing nothing. When researchers measured the energy a moon jellyfish spends per distance traveled, they recorded the lowest cost of transport of any animal ever tested. It is not fast. It was never trying to be fast. It is cheap, and in an ocean where food arrives unpredictably, cheap outlives quick. Even its relationship with time is negotiable. Turritopsis dohrnii, a jellyfish smaller than your fingernail, responds to injury or starvation by reversing its own development, dissolving its adult form and reverting to the polyp stage from which it originally grew. It can then start the cycle again. It is not immortal in any useful sense, since predators and disease still find it, but it is the only known animal that can decline to finish growing up. This is where the story stops being charming. Jellyfish do well in oceans that are warming, overfished, and short of oxygen, because those conditions ruin their competitors and leave their food untouched. In 2013 a swarm of moon jellyfish blocked the cooling water intake of a Swedish nuclear plant and forced a reactor offline. Read that again. An animal with no brain shut down a reactor. It did not scheme, or target, or intend. It drifted where the current took it, in the numbers it has always come in, and we had built something in the way. We are used to reading the ocean as a hierarchy with intelligence at the top, and we are used to placing ourselves at the summit of it. The jellyfish has been quietly ignoring that hierarchy since before there was anything on land worth looking at. The lesson is not that brains are useless. The lesson is that they are one solution among several, and not obviously the most patient one.
